5, 7; to be born, i. q. Niph. Judg. 13, 8.
Ps. 87, 4. 5. 6. With לְ of father Gen.
4, 26. 24, 15. Judg. 18, 29; with בֵּן impl.
Gen. 10, 21. So with לְ of a near rela-
tive, Ruth 4, 17 יֻלַּד־בֵּן לְנָעֳמִי. Is. 9, 5;
לְ of thing Job 5, 7.—Trop. to be brought
forth, created, e. g. the mountains, Ps.
Hiph. הוֹלִיד 1. to cause to bring
forth, as God a woman Is. 66, 9; a man
his wife, to make fruitful, to have chil-
dren by her, 1 Chr. 2, 18. 8, 8.—Trop.
of rain as fertilizing the earth Is. 55, 10.
2. to beget, as a father, i. q. Kal no. 2;
Ecc. 6, 3. al.—Trop. to create, Job 38, 28
מִי־הוֹלִיד אֶגְלֵי־טָל who hath begotten
(created) the store-houses of the dew?
3. i. q. Kal no. 1, to bear, to bring
forth; but only trop. to bring forth
wickedness, Is. 59, 4; parall. הָרָה עָמָל.
Hoph. pr. ‘to be begotten,’ hence to
be born. Inf. הֻלֶּדֶת Gen. 40, 20. Ez. 16,
5, and הוּלֶּדֶת Ez. 16, 4, a being born,
birth, nativity. Gen. l. c. יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת אֶת־
פַּרְעֹה the birth-day of Pharaoh, pr. the
day of Pharaoh’s being born. On the
accus. with passives, see Heb. Gr. § 140.
Hithpa. to declare one’s birth or de-
scent, pedigree; to give one’s name to
be enrolled in genealogical tables, Num.
1, 18.—In the later books this idea is
expressed by הִתְיַחֵשׂ.
Deriv. יָלִיד, מוֹלֶדֶת, תּוֹלֶדֶת; pr. names
מוֹלִיד, מוֹלָדָה, תּוֹלָד, אֶלְתּוֹלָד; and the
four here following.
יֶלֶד m. in pause יָלֶד; plur. יְלָדִים,
constr. יַלְדֵי, once יִלְדֵי Is. 57, 4.
1. one born, a son, poet. i. q. בֵּן; spoken
κατ᾿ ἐξοχήν of the king’s son Is. 9, 5.
Hence יַלְדֵי נָכְרִים sons of strangers,
poet. for foreigners, see בֵּן no. 1; also
sons of transgression, for transgressors,
Is. 57, 4.—Plur. comm. children, i. q.
also for the young of animals, Is. 11, 7.
2. a boy, child, recently born, an in-
fant, Ex. 1, 17. 2, 3 sq. Ruth 4, 16.
2 Sam. 12, 15 sq. 1 K. 3, 25; as borne in
the arms Gen. 21, 8; also as older and
mingling in childish sports 2 K. 2, 24.
Job 21, 11. Zech. 8, 5; but still of tender
age Gen. 33, 13. Is. 57, 5. Also as more
advanced, a youth, young man, Gen. 4,
23 parall. אִישׁ. 37, 30. 42, 22 of Joseph
when 17 years old. Dan. 1, 4. 10. 1 K.
יַלְדָּה fem. of יֶלֶד, a girl, maiden,
Gen. 34, 4. Joel 4, 3. Plur. יְלָדוֹת Zech.
יַלְדוּת f. (denom. from יֶלֶד) childhood,
youth, Ecc. 11, 9. 10.—Concr. youth, for
young men, Ps. 110, 3.
יִלּוֹד adj. verbal, born, i. q. יָלוּד, Ex.
יָלוֹן (passing the night, abiding, r.
לוּן) Jalon, pr. n. m. 1 Chr. 4, 17.
יָלִיד m. (r. יָלַד) 1. Adj. verbal, born,
chiefly in the phrase יְלִיד בַּיִת one born
in the house, a house-born slave, verna,
Jer. 2, 14. Arab. وَلِيدٌ, تَلِيدٌ, id.
2. Subst. a son, child, יְלִידֵי הָעֲנָק the
sons of Anak Num. 13, 22. 28; יְלִידֵי
הָרָפָה the sons of Rapha, i. q. רְפָאִים
Rephaim, 2 Sam. 21, 16. 18.
* יָלַךְ to go, see הָלַךְ.
* יָלַל not used in Kal, onomatopoetic,
to yell, to wail, Arab. وَلْوَلَ, Syr. and
Zab. ܐܝܠܠ, Chald. יְלֵל Aph. אַיְלֵל.
Kindred roots are אָלַל II, אָלָה, Gr.
ὀλολύζειν, Lat. ejulare, ululare, Engl.
to yell; also Armen. lal, Germ. lullen,
Engl. to lull.
Hiph. הֵילִיל; fut. יֵילִיל Mic. 1, 8;
oftener יְיֵלִיל Is. 15, 2. 3, from the form
יְהֵילִילוּ Is. 52, 5; ה between two vowels
being softened to י.
1. to wail, to lament, Jer. 47, 2. Ez.
21, 17. al. With עַל of that over or for
which, Jer. 48, 31. 51, 8. Mic. 1, 8; לְ id.
Is. 16, 7.—Ascribed also to inanimate
things, as trees Zech. 11, 2; places, as
filled with wailings, הֵילִילִי שַׁעַר Is. 14, 31.
23, 1. Often in prophetic denunciations
Zeph. 1, 11. Amos 8, 3 הֵילִילוּ שִׁירוֹת הֵיכָל
the songs of the palace wail, are turned
to wailings.
2. Once of the exulting cries of
haughty victors, to yell, to shout, Lat.
ululare, Is. 52, 5. So أهلّ of a warlike

line_status.note: A short horizontal stroke at top-line height joins the dalet of יֻלַּד to the following bet — a printed maqqef (יֻלַּד־בֵּן), not a word space; the rest of the line (vowels, dagesh in lamed and bet, לְנָעֳמִי with hataf-qamets) is identical in both readings.

The opening quotation mark sits directly against "to" with only normal type-side bearing, not a printed space; Reading B's "‘ to" inserts a space that is not in the print. Everything else is identical in both readings.
The printed left-to-right order after "Deriv." is יָלִיד, מוֹלֶדֶת, תּוֹלֶדֶת (Reading A reversed it), and the lamed of תּוֹלֶדֶת carries segol (three dots), not tsere as in A.
The vowel under the final lamed of אֶלְתּוֹלָד is a qamets (T-shaped, matching the preceding תּוֹלָד), not a pathach as in Reading A.

The elision mark after κατ is printed as the Greek typographic psili/koronis-shaped apostrophe, not a straight ASCII apostrophe; B's U+1FBF matches that (U+2019 would be an equally acceptable rendering). Everything else is identical in both readings and correct.

In the second Hebrew word the dot on the vav sits at mid-height (shureq, יָלוּד = passive participle), not above the letter as the holem clearly does in the first word יִלּוֹד; Reading B's יָלוֹד is wrong.

The word after "Zab." is set in Syriac Estrangela type (alaph, yod, lamadh, lamadh = ܐܝܠܠ), not Mandaic script as Reading A gives; Reading B has the right script and letters. The Chaldee forms יְלֵל and אַיְלֵל match the print exactly. Caveat: there are two small marks above the Syriac word (one over the alaph, one over the lamadhs) that may be Syriac vowel points, but they are too indistinct in this scan to identify with confidence, so they are not encoded.

The Arabic word has three letter-bodies (hamza-alif, medial hā', final lām with shadda); Reading A omits the hā' (أَلَّ), which the print does not support. No fatḥas are printed beyond the hamza and shadda.
